newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan parliament dissolved for October 20 election.
newsitem.headline: Japan parliament dissolved for October 20 election.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday dissolved parliament and set October 20 as the date for general elections expected to bring about political realignment but no major policy changes.

The prospect of elections for the 500-seat Lower House, the first since July 1993 polls ended 38 years of unbroken rule by the Liberal Democratic Party and ushered in an era of coalition government, has so far failed to excite an apathetic public.

Most analysts expect a record-low turnout for a heated but issue-free contest as weeks of wrangling between Hashimoto's LDP and two smaller coalition partners over timing of the polls gives way to an LDP search for post-election partners.

One point of focus is whether the LDP, which regained the reins of power in 1994 in a coalition with the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake, can capture a simple majority or will be forced to shop for new coalition partners.
Hashimoto, who is also LDP president, urged his party to fight to give him a second term unfettered by the need to compromise with coalition partners.
"Although the LDP has been the biggest party over the last three years, we still don't have a simple majority," he said.
Hashimoto is expected to pin his bid for a second term on an improving economy and his handling of a bitter dispute with the southern prefecture of Okinawa over U.S. military bases.
The opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), headed by former LDP powerbroker Ichiro Ozawa, plans to attack the government over an unpopular sales tax rise due in April.
Shinshinto, made of components of the reformist government that ruled briefly in 1993-94, will also offer a plan for a drastic tax-system overhaul and to cut bureaucratic red tape.
To Shinshinto's chagrin -- and widespread public scepticism -- the LDP has also adopted administrative reform as its poll platform, making it hard for voters to compare platforms.
Marketwatchers said the elections would be a mere sideshow to more critical economic factors, but did not rule out bursts of hopeful anticipation.

"In the days leading to the election, there will be many optimistic promises of change with the aim of wooing voters and that could nourish the stock market," said Yasuo Ueki, general manager at Nikko Securities.
But Hashimoto's pep talk to the LDP on Friday offered a hint that he stands more for continuity than drastic change.
"We are heading for a storm of reform, and our politics, administration and social system must weather it," he told LDP legislators.
Analysts say the LDP will fall some 20-30 seats short of a simple majority, forcing it to forge a coalition with a smaller party with reformist credentials.
The Democratic Party, a new 40-strong group of defectors from the Social Democrats and Sakigake which boasts maverick Health Minister Naoto Kan as one of its members, fits the bill, analysts say.

Kan, who aims to make the Democrats a vehicle to attract urban voters disappointed with established parties, achieved hero status this year when he revealed health ministry complicity in a decades-old scandal in which the AIDS virus was spread through untreated blood products.

"Stagnation would come if the LDP gets a simple majority," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research Institute. "The economy would like a strong plurality for the LDP, with Kan and the Democrats there to hold Hashimoto's feet to the fire on reform."

The polls will be the first under reforms enacted in 1994 to correct a gerrymandered system which heavily favoured rural districts over urban areas and was seen as one reason for the long domination of Japanese politics by the LDP.
Under the new system, candidates will contest 300 seats in single-seat constituencies, with the other 200 seats decided through proportional representation.
